claims.text: A modest increase in Ni concentration in a tungsten-based high-entropy alloy will improve its lattice heat-transfer capability.
Coherent nanoprecipitates will preserve the alloy's mechanical integrity under high-temperature plasma-facing conditions.
The initial tungsten-based refractory HEA is strengthened by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations.
Ni can be increased while Cu is reduced without disrupting coherent nanoprecipitate formation.
Temperatures up to about 800 °C are relevant to the proposed plasma-facing application.
The proposed behavior will hold under high thermal flux and fusion-reactor-like irradiation.
Coherent nanoprecipitate interfaces facilitate dislocation transmission or mobility.
Coherent nanoprecipitate interfaces reduce stress concentrations associated with premature crack initiation.
Increasing Ni raises lattice thermal conductivity by promoting higher-frequency phonon modes.
The Ni-associated phonon modes have greater group velocities.
Increasing Ni reduces phonon scattering in the proposed tungsten-based alloy.
Coherent nanoprecipitates protect the alloy against thermal and irradiation-induced degradation.
The modified alloy will have higher lattice thermal conductivity than the baseline alloy.
The modified alloy will maintain tensile strength under reactor-relevant operating conditions.
The modified alloy will maintain phase stability under reactor-relevant operating conditions.
The baseline equiatomic tungsten-based HEA has moderate thermal conductivity.
The baseline tungsten-based alloy has excellent mechanical properties because of its nanoprecipitate-stabilized microstructure.
Prior experiments supporting the boundary included simulated plasma flux and irradiation from ambient temperature to approximately 800 °C.
Increasing Ni by 5–10% relative to the standard composition is a suitable systematic intervention range.
